routes.description: Establish that humans are personally accountable under a trustworthy divine moral order, that judgment answers genuine guilt, and that Christ's substitutionary death and resurrection make merciful salvation coherent through repentance and faith.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine authority and human culpability are adequately grounded, punishment and substitution are shown to be morally intelligible, and repentance, faith, grace, and resurrection form a coherent account of salvation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the account of sin, judgment, atonement, and salvation into a morally and explanatorily coherent gospel.

centralBridges.description: Ground God's moral authority and show that human beings bear personal guilt for their own wrongdoing.
Explain why judgment is deserved and how Christ's substitution permits mercy without abandoning justice.
Specify how repentance, faith, grace, resurrection, and personal transformation provide salvation rather than moral works.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply a warrant for trusting God, scripture, creation, conscience, and claimed transformative experience.
Reconcile divine foreknowledge and a fallen creation with individual responsibility and confidence in divine justice.

routes.description: Show that the gospel account fails moral or explanatory scrutiny because responsibility is misassigned, substitution does not resolve wrongdoing, divine alternatives appear less harmful, and its foundational and salvific claims lack reliable evidential support.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if central features of guilt, judgment, atonement, or salvation are shown to be unjustified, internally unstable, needlessly designed, or dependent on methods that cannot reliably establish their truth.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that the proposed account of sin, atonement, and salvation does not jointly satisfy moral and explanatory standards.

centralBridges.description: Test whether inherited guilt and an omniscient creator's choices are compatible with personal culpability and just punishment.
Test whether sacrificial substitution is necessary, morally permissible, and capable of addressing defective character or repeated wrongdoing.
Require non-circular, discriminating support for God, scripture, resurrection, and the claimed operation of salvation.
Compare the gospel's history of suffering, hiddenness, judgment, and rescue with less harmful divine alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Determine whether conversion and salvation claims permit adverse experience to count against them.
Distinguish evidence-proportioned confidence from faith, assertion, assumed design, and appeals to humility.

sections.title: Human Guilt, Divine Foreknowledge, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: The justice of sin and judgment depends on whether people are accountable for their conduct despite inherited conditions, divine foreknowledge, creative choice, and the availability of alternative worlds.

sections.title: Substitutionary Atonement, Forgiveness, and Moral Repair
sections.rationale: This issue directly tests whether Christ's sacrifice is necessary and just, whether penalty payment can ground forgiveness, and whether substitution addresses the wrongdoer's underlying moral condition.

sections.title: Evidence for God, Scripture, and Resurrection
sections.rationale: The gospel's explanation requires support for its divine lawgiver, scriptural authority, and resurrection claims, making the dispute over creation, revelation, faith, and evidential standards structurally central.

sections.title: Repentance, Faith, Conversion, and the Salvation Promise
sections.rationale: The account must explain how salvation is obtained and known while addressing whether failed conversion, continued nonbelief, or contrary experience can meaningfully test its promises.

sections.title: Suffering, Divine Hiddenness, and the Design of Judgment
sections.rationale: The moral and explanatory adequacy of the gospel also turns on whether a fallen world, divine absence, severe suffering, and ultimate punishment fit a wise and just salvific plan.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: God's moral law establishes human guilt, while Jesus's death pays the guilty person's penalty and thereby permits a judge to forgive without abandoning justice.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Ray the floor, and the uninterrupted opening statement is spoken in Ray's first-person evangelical voice.

response.rationale: Constructive presentation of the principal guilt, penalty, substitution, and forgiveness mechanism; no earlier opposing target applies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a complete central mechanism, though its legal analogy compresses important moral warrants.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but movement among fine, penalty, guilt, and divine judgment leaves a material partly stable element.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The court-fine analogy is asserted as establishing the atonement mechanism without qualifying differences between transferable debts and personal culpability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy supplies a recognizable inference, but the transferability of a monetary fine to moral punishment remains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion relies chiefly on scriptural assertion and a courtroom analogy without independent support for divine law, guilt, or substitution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly connects guilt, judgment, atonement, and forgiveness to the motion-level gospel-coherence condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents its own account rather than interpreting a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says humanity violated God's law, Jesus paid the fine, and a judge may then forgive justly.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: The gospel becomes intelligible when a person humbly acknowledges serious sin, repents, and trusts the risen Christ for eternal life as God's gift.
moves.attributionBasis: Ray remains the sole speaker throughout this concluding portion of his opening and explicitly states his gospel conclusion and appeal to Matt.

response.rationale: Constructive statement of the proposed salvation path through acknowledged sin, repentance, trust, resurrection, and divine gift.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the route clearly but gives limited explanation of how the conditions produce or verify salvation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The salvation conditions are recoverable, but the scope of the claim that pride explains gospel unintelligibility is not expressly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted salvation promise and explanation of dissent exceed the support supplied in the excerpt and omit rival explanations.

charity.alternative: A person may understand the gospel yet reject it for evidential or moral reasons rather than pride.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not distinguish unwillingness to acknowledge sin from informed disagreement about the gospel's truth.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Repentance and trust form an intelligible conditional account, but the bridge from those acts to eternal life is substantially assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Resurrection, divine gift, and the psychological diagnosis of nonacceptance are asserted rather than independently supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the motion-level connection between sin, atonement, resurrection, and salvation.

representationalCharity.rationale: It materially narrows nonacceptance to pride without handling the strongest reasonable alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt links Christ's death and resurrection, the gift of eternal life, acknowledgment of sin, repentance, and trust.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Original sin cannot fairly be assigned to humanity if an omniscient God knowingly chose a creation in which human disobedience was inevitable despite having alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has handed the floor to Matt, and this passage occurs within Matt's uninterrupted opening critique of the gospel message.

components.text: Whether God's moral law makes each person personally guilty for that person's own violations.
Whether divine judgment and condemnation are just given the source of the relevant guilt.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges divine responsibility for original sin, but the targeted pro move grounded guilt in personal lawbreaking rather than inherited guilt or inevitability; it therefore contacts a related justice component without answering the decisive personal-violation premise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it offers substantial contrary material but does not contact the selected target's decisive personal-guilt claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument expressly conditions responsibility on omniscience, available alternatives, and inevitability, keeping its scope clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional questions acknowledge uncertainty, though the conclusion that God thereby brings original sin remains somewhat stronger than the undeveloped modal premise.

charity.alternative: Foreknowledge need not cause human choices, and creatures may remain responsible for choices God knowingly permits.
charity.decisiveQualification: The challenge concerns God's prior choice among available creations, not foreknowledge alone, but it does not fully resolve concurrent creature responsibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given omniscience, alternatives, and inevitability, assigning substantial design responsibility to God follows, though exclusive responsibility does not.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reasoning is conditional and needs no empirical proof of the stated hypothetical, but the availability and nature of alternatives are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central responsibility bridge concerning omniscient creation and personal culpability.

representationalCharity.rationale: It targets a strong permission-and-alternatives account while leaving one important responsibility qualification compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether sin was inevitable, whether God knew beforehand, and whether God could have created differently.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Inherited sin is morally incoherent because it assigns people guilt and punishment for conduct committed by other people before they were born.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Matt's continuous opening statement and is framed through his personal analogy about receiving undeserved punishment.

response.rationale: Constructive moral critique of inherited guilt; no earlier opposing target is required for this locked constructive move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states a direct principle and applies it clearly, with only limited treatment of alternative doctrines.

precisionFindings.rationale: Inherited guilt is consistently distinguished from wrongdoing personally committed by the person punished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The moral conclusion is proportionate to the explicitly described case of guilt assigned solely for another person's prior act.

charity.alternative: Original sin may describe inherited corruption or consequences rather than personal guilt for Adam's act.
charity.decisiveQualification: The argument succeeds against inherited guilt as stated but does not by itself defeat every doctrine of inherited condition or consequence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from nonparticipation in another's act to the injustice of personal guilt is clear and contains only a bounded doctrinal qualification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim rests on a well-specified moral distinction and apt analogy, though it does not compare competing accounts of original sin.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central bridge testing inherited guilt and just punishment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly criticizes the expressed guilt claim, though it does not expressly preserve this doctrinal distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly describes people as born guilty for acts done before their birth and distinguishes those acts from their own conduct.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Jesus's sacrifice is an unnecessary blood ritual because a rule-making and enforcing God could forgive without requiring a sacrifice of himself to himself.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt delivers this entire passage during his opening, consistently using first-person skeptical analysis of sacrifice, divine rules, and available evidence.

components.text: Whether a just God needs Jesus to pay a penalty before forgiving guilty people.
Whether the court-fine analogy makes sacrificial substitution morally intelligible.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges both the necessity and intelligibility of the penalty-payment mechanism by asking why the divine rule-maker could not forgive without self-sacrifice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it expressly contacts the decisive necessity and substitution premises of the earlier move.

precisionFindings.rationale: The core necessity objection is clear, but the rhetorical label 'blood magic' is less stable and broader than the specified sacrificial mechanism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The question appropriately shifts a necessity burden, though calling the practice nonsensical precedes a full comparison with possible justice-based answers.

charity.alternative: A perfectly just God might have principled reasons to require satisfaction rather than simply waive punishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro move must explain those reasons and the moral permissibility of substitution; divine rule-making power alone does not conclusively show there are none.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument validly exposes an unexplained necessity in the proposed mechanism, with a bounded gap concerning constraints internal to perfect justice.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual challenge is supported by God's stipulated rule-making authority, but competing accounts of forgiveness and justice are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: By attacking a central atonement component as unnecessary, it directly advances the motion-level gospel critique.

representationalCharity.rationale: It presses the strongest unexplained necessity issue but compresses the principled-justice alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt characterizes Jesus as a special blood sacrifice and explicitly asks why God cannot simply forgive.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A wise and powerful God seeking fellowship could create suitable people with him directly, making the history of suffering, damnation, and rescue needlessly inefficient.
moves.attributionBasis: This is an uninterrupted strategic critique in Matt's opening, explicitly introduced as an examination of what God's goal and plan might be.

response.rationale: Constructive design comparison proposing direct creation with God as a less harmful route to the stated fellowship goal.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it frames a clear alternative, though its feasibility and preservation of relevant goods are compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly conditional on fellowship being God's goal and identifies the proposed alternative.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents possible divine goals and a comparative question rather than claiming certainty about God's actual purpose.

charity.alternative: Earthly history may enable freedom, character formation, or relationships unavailable through direct creation in God's presence.
charity.decisiveQualification: A successful alternative must preserve whatever independently justified goods the proposed history uniquely supplies.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The means-end critique is coherent under its stated goal, but it leaves a material bridge about whether the alternative preserves relevant goods.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparison is a plausible conceptual challenge, yet the feasibility and consequences of the alternative world remain largely stipulated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central design bridge by comparing the gospel history with an allegedly less harmful alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move invites comparison but does not fully examine the strongest good-preservation response.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly asks God's goal and proposes creating willing companions directly with God rather than through the existing process.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: If earthly life is intended to teach people, God's absence makes it inferior to instruction by an available teacher and therefore evidence of a poorly designed plan.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt continues his uninterrupted opening and marks this as another possible account of God's goal before developing the classroom and sandwich analogies.

response.rationale: Constructive hiddenness and design argument comparing an absent divine teacher with ordinary available instruction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, the analogy clearly presents the challenge but only briefly connects teaching quality to the complete salvific plan.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is explicitly conditional on earthly life serving a teaching purpose and consistently compares instructional designs.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The classroom analogy supports a presumptive comparison, but 'better' instruction depends on goals and constraints left unstated.

charity.alternative: Divine hiddenness may preserve autonomy or make indirect moral learning possible in a way overt instruction would not.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those benefits require defense and comparison against the costs of ambiguity and error.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The instructor analogy yields a coherent prima facie design criticism, though the equivalence between classroom instruction and divine formation is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary teaching practice supports the comparison, but no evidence establishes that divine teaching has the same goals or constraints.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central design bridge concerning hiddenness and the quality of the salvific plan.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move leaves room for multiple goals and fairly poses the comparison, with one omitted qualification about autonomy.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts an actual guiding instructor with students receiving only beliefs about what an absent teacher wants investigated.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: God has supplied moral knowledge through a divinely given conscience whose operation persists despite social shaping and the possibility that it becomes seared.
moves.attributionBasis: Ray explicitly begins answering Matt's claim about missing signs, and his answer continues across Matt's brief challenges until Ray's question about stealing.

components.text: Whether God's absence makes the proposed teaching plan inferior to instruction by an available teacher.
Whether people possess any divinely supplied guidance despite the teacher's apparent absence.

response.rationale: A God-given conscience supplies relevant alleged guidance, but the move does not compare that mechanism with an available teacher or answer the argument about instructional quality and hiddenness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it contacts the secondary guidance issue but leaves the decisive comparative-design demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conscience claim is recoverable, but 'seared' is metaphorical and the extent to which conscience survives social variation is unclear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The divine origin and diagnostic operation of conscience are stated certainly despite acknowledged differences and no independent support.

charity.alternative: Conscience may be socially and psychologically formed and may differ sincerely across people.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling disagreement a seared conscience does not discriminate divine moral knowledge from ordinary variation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The searing explanation is compatible with variation but risks circularly treating counterexamples as damage, leaving a substantial inference gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Divine origin is supported by scriptural assertion and analogy, while the admitted variation is not independently explained.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies a claimed warrant for conscience, placing it high within the subsidiary burden tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges variation but explains it through the favored account without addressing the strongest rival explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt acknowledges differing consciences, invokes the biblical idea of searing, and claims God's law can expose the remaining conscience.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A scriptural assertion about another person's inner knowledge cannot override that person's contrary report or independently establish the assertion's truth.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt states the objection before and after Ray's intervening appeal to an inspired instruction book, making the responsive ownership and conclusion explicit.

components.text: Whether scriptural claims about a person's conscience independently establish that person's suppressed moral or divine knowledge.
Whether disagreement can be explained as a seared conscience despite the person's contrary report.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the circular evidential defect: the book's assertion about another person's inner state cannot establish its own authority or override contrary testimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it identifies the decisive evidential failure and its consequence for the asserted inner-state claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between a book's assertion, a person's report, and independent truth-establishment remains clear throughout.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The narrow claim that assertion alone cannot independently establish its truth is supported without extending to the impossibility of all scriptural evidence.

charity.alternative: Scripture may be independently warranted and therefore capable of correcting mistaken self-assessment.
charity.decisiveQualification: That independent warrant must be supplied rather than inferred from the scripture's own assertion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument cleanly distinguishes asserted content from independent warrant and states the defeating consequence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The exchange itself supplies specific evidence of the circular appeal, with only broader scriptural warrant outside the narrow claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central evidence bridge by requiring non-circular support for scripture and claimed inner knowledge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately preserves the strongest alternative while identifying the missing independent warrant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes the scriptural claim, identifies the instruction book as its basis, and challenges the inference that the book cannot be wrong.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: Divine foreknowledge and original sin do not excuse personal wrongdoing, just as blaming God would not remove a guilty defendant's responsibility for a serious crime.
moves.attributionBasis: Ray explicitly announces that he will address Matt's argument and delivers the continuous courtroom analogy in his own voice.

components.text: Whether an omniscient creator who had alternatives bears responsibility for knowingly choosing a world with inevitable sin.
Whether a person remains responsible for serious wrongdoing personally committed despite inherited conditions.
Whether human perpetrators retain personal responsibility for their own acts.

response.rationale: The courtroom analogy establishes that blaming God does not automatically erase the actor's responsibility, but it does not answer the decisive creator-choice argument or the separate objection to guilt inherited for another's acts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it strongly contacts retained human responsibility while leaving divine design responsibility unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The personal-responsibility point is clear, but the analogy slides from an extreme crime to all sin without stating the scope conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy strongly rebuts total excuse but is presented as if it also resolved the distinct foreknowledge and inherited-guilt objections.

charity.alternative: God and the human actor may bear different or concurrent forms of responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that the actor remains responsible does not remove the creator's alleged design responsibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy supports retained actor responsibility, but treating that as a resolution of creator responsibility is a substantial non sequitur.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary legal responsibility supports the narrow point, but the extreme hypothetical does not warrant the broader theological conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central responsibility bridge, although it answers only one component of that burden.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially weakens the objection into a claim of complete human excuse and omits concurrent responsibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly answers the prior argument with a defendant who blames God and original sin for a serious personally committed crime.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: A former profession of Christianity followed by departure does not disconfirm the gospel's promise if the person never genuinely repented and therefore underwent a false conversion.
moves.attributionBasis: Ray answers the request for a way to know he is right and directly applies his false-conversion account to Matt by name.

components.text: Whether an authority's assertion about another person's inner state can override contrary testimony or independently establish truth.

response.rationale: The false-conversion diagnosis repeats the disputed inference about Matt's inner repentance rather than supplying an independent basis for knowing that diagnosis or answering the circularity challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it applies contrary material to the same issue but leaves the decisive epistemic demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional proposition is clear, but 'true repentance' lacks an independently specified criterion in the excerpt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker asserts certainty about another person's past inner state without discriminating evidence and treats departure as confirmation.

charity.alternative: A person may have sincerely believed and repented by the community's available standards before later becoming unconvinced.
charity.decisiveQualification: A false-conversion diagnosis requires evidence independent of the later departure it is used to explain.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account is usable as a possibility, but as disconfirmation it is self-sealing because departure supplies both the challenge and the diagnosis.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim about Matt's past repentance is unsupported and contradicts his report without an independent verification criterion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary falsifiability burden by offering a way to classify adverse conversion experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument depends on dismissing the strongest sincere-conversion alternative without independent examination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt tells Matt that his conversion was false, that he did not truly repent, and that later trial exposed the defect.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A former Christian's present disbelief does not show that the former belief was insincere, and reclassifying that belief as false does not establish Christianity's truth.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt explicitly distinguishes an actual divine relationship from sincere belief and supports the latter attribution with testimony from people who knew him.

components.text: Whether later departure establishes that the former profession lacked genuine repentance or conversion.
Whether labeling the earlier conversion false provides evidence that Christianity is true.

response.rationale: The reply directly identifies that present disbelief does not entail past insincerity and that reclassification of the conversion does not establish the religion's truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly attacks the inference and states both evidential consequences.

precisionFindings.rationale: It carefully distinguishes sincere belief from an actual divine relationship and limits supporting testimony to sincerity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move does not claim to prove a real divine relationship; it makes the narrower, supported claim about sincere former belief.

charity.alternative: A conversion may appear sincere externally while lacking the theology's required inward repentance.
charity.decisiveQualification: That possibility does not establish the diagnosis and needs independent criteria and evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between sincerity, truth, and later belief is explicit and defeats the targeted entailment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Personal testimony is corroborated by contemporaneous acquaintances, though it cannot independently prove every inward feature.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary falsifiability bridge at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the distinction between apparent sincerity and theological genuineness while locating the unresolved burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites former church acquaintances who regarded Matt as devout and explains that a false-Christian label does not show Christianity true.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: The existence of creation is self-evident evidence of a creator in the same way that a building or painting evidences its maker.
moves.attributionBasis: Ray rejects the characterization that Matt refuses belief and immediately states the creator argument through two explicit maker analogies.

components.text: Whether a former believer's present disbelief entails that the earlier conversion was insincere or false.
Whether there is evidence for God apart from assertions about another person's inner state.

response.rationale: The maker analogies offer relevant contrary evidence for a creator but do not address the selected target's decisive former-conversion inference or establish scriptural authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it supplies a distinct evidential consideration but leaves the primary conversion demand untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: 'Creation' presupposes the disputed maker-like classification, and the analogy's scope from artifacts to the universe is unqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move calls creation proof of a creator although the artifact analogy alone does not establish the universe's relevant similarity or a specific creator.

charity.alternative: Buildings and paintings are known artifacts, while treating the universe as an artifact is the disputed conclusion.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy needs independent features that justify extending maker inference to the universe.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogical form is intelligible, but the crucial similarity between artifacts and the total natural order is substantially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Familiar artifact examples do not independently establish cosmic design, the biblical God, or scriptural truth.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central evidence burden by offering purported evidence for a creator.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move omits the strongest category-difference objection and largely assumes the design classification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The complete short excerpt states that creation proves a creator and supports this with building-builder and painting-painter analogies.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Faith cannot demonstrate God, divine lawgiving, or scriptural truth and therefore is not a reliable method for establishing the gospel's foundational claims.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty explicitly describes his epistemic objections and closes by stating that Comfort has not proved the claims.

components.text: Whether maker analogies and faith demonstrate a creator, divine lawgiver, judge, or scriptural truth.
Whether asserted divine origins of moral knowledge have a truth-establishing warrant.
Whether trust in Christ supplies a reliable epistemic route to the gospel's truth.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies the missing demonstration and states the defeating consequence that faith, as presented, is not a discriminating pathway to truth for the foundational claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly contacts the evidence demand and explains why the offered method does not establish the conclusions.

precisionFindings.rationale: Faith is evaluated specifically as a method for demonstrating named foundational claims, not dismissed in every possible role.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is appropriately limited to faith without demonstration and matches the evidential deficiency identified.

charity.alternative: Faith may be trust grounded in evidence rather than belief without evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The relevant evidence must still be supplied and shown to discriminate the claimed God and scriptures from rivals.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from nondiscriminating assertion to failure as a truth method is clear and directly tied to the named claims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The debate exchange specifically exhibits the unsupported appeals challenged, with only a bounded omission of a broader reliability comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level critique that the gospel's foundational claims lack a reliable truth method.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move focuses on the actual unsupported use of faith, though it does not expressly distinguish every evidence-grounded conception.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names God, divine lawgiving, judgment, and scriptural truth, says they cannot be demonstrated there, and rejects faith as a sound epistemology.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: Pervasive suffering, disease, natural disaster, and death corroborate the biblical teaching that humanity inhabits a fallen creation.
moves.attributionBasis: Comfort directly answers the audience's problem-of-evil question by repeatedly appealing to scripture and fallen creation.

components.text: Whether God could achieve the proposed salvific or fellowship goal through a less harmful creative alternative.
Whether suffering and hiddenness fit a well-designed divine teaching plan.
Whether observed suffering independently warrants the truth of the scriptural fallen-creation account.

response.rationale: The move redescribes suffering as predicted by fallen-creation doctrine but does not compare alternatives, explain the design, or show that the observations discriminate scripture from rival accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it contacts a secondary evidential issue while leaving the decisive alternative-design demand unaddressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but 'substantiate' equivocates between compatibility, prediction, and discriminating confirmation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Compatibility of suffering with a fallen world is treated as confirmation without comparing how expected suffering is under rival hypotheses.

charity.alternative: Suffering may be compatible with a fallen creation yet equally or better explained by naturalistic or alternative theological accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Corroboration requires comparative expectation, not mere consistency with scripture.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The observation is compatible with the doctrine, but inferring substantive confirmation without comparative expectations is a substantial evidential gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples of suffering are specific, but they do not discriminate the fallen-creation explanation from serious alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central design critique by claiming suffering fits the biblical account, though it does not make the requested comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move omits the decisive rival-explanation qualification and treats adverse facts as straightforward support.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists cancer, disasters, pain, and death, then says those phenomena substantiate scripture's fallen-creation teaching.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Paying another person's debt can remove an obligation but does not repair the wrongdoer's defective character or prevent that person from repeating the wrongdoing.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty develops the debt and broken-window analogies after being asked to explain the question's implication.

components.text: Whether payment of another person's penalty resolves the morally relevant problem created by wrongdoing.
Whether the salvation mechanism includes repair of the wrongdoer's defective character.
Whether personal responsibility persists after another party addresses consequences.

response.rationale: The reply accepts that payment can remove an obligation but diagnoses the failure to repair character or prevent repetition, directly limiting what the payment analogy can establish.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it targets the analogy's decisive inference and states the unresolved moral consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move expressly distinguishes discharged obligation, repaired victim loss, wrongdoer character, and repeated conduct.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that third-party payment alone does not reform character follows from the stated analogies.

charity.alternative: Atonement may be paired with repentance, sanctification, and transformation rather than functioning as payment alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those additional mechanisms must be supplied; the payment analogy itself does not provide moral repair.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between compensating an obligation and reforming the wrongdoer is explicit, consistent, and defeats the analogy's overreach.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The debt and broken-window examples are specific and representative for the narrow conceptual distinction, with only broader theological comparison omitted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level critique by challenging the atonement mechanism's capacity for moral repair.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument accurately limits its objection to what payment alone accomplishes and leaves room for supplementary transformation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes replacement of a broken window from reforming the person who continues breaking windows and applies that distinction to debt payment.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: Christianity treats people as guilty before a holy judge and offers salvation through divine mercy made legally possible by Christ's sacrificial death and resurrection rather than by good works.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator finishes reading a question to Ray, after which Ray gives a sustained answer using his characteristic first-person evangelical presentation.

components.text: Whether sacrificial payment repairs the wrongdoer's character or prevents repeated wrongdoing.
Whether sacrifice is required for mercy rather than direct forgiveness.
Whether payment can remove judicial liability before a holy judge.

response.rationale: The answer restates guilt, judgment, mercy, and sacrifice and contrasts grace with works, but it never answers the decisive character-repair objection and only asserts the necessity of sacrifice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it contacts judicial liability and necessity but leaves the primary moral-repair component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The judicial-mercy account is clear, with only an implicit limitation that it concerns standing before God rather than full character transformation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts divine judgment and sacrifice as the mechanism making mercy possible without defending necessity or moral transferability.

charity.alternative: Good works need not purchase forgiveness, while forgiveness may still occur without penal substitution and may require moral repair.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting works-righteousness does not establish sacrifice as necessary or sufficient.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The internal judicial model is intelligible, but the necessity of sacrifice and its relation to transformation remain material unsupported bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account rests on biblical assertion and judicial framing without comparative support against direct forgiveness or restorative alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly connects guilt, judgment, sacrifice, mercy, resurrection, and salvation at the motion tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move substitutes a contrast with works for the strongest objections about direct forgiveness and transformation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts attempted good works with guilty criminals before a holy judge and presents mercy through Christ's sacrifice and resurrection.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: Sinners deserve the loss imposed at judgment, and where human reason cannot resolve the severity of that outcome, God's righteousness warrants trust that he will act justly.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Ray whether sinners deserve unending torment, and the ensuing uninterrupted answer uses Ray's theological claims and cited preacher.

components.text: Whether a wise and powerful God could select a less harmful plan than severe judgment and rescue.
Whether trust without a worked-out justification is a reliable basis for the justice claim.
Whether severe outcomes fit a well-designed teaching or salvific plan.

response.rationale: The move asserts desert and trust in divine righteousness but neither compares less harmful alternatives nor supplies a reason why the severe outcome is proportionate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it acknowledges the unresolved reason-demand but replaces it with trust rather than contacting the decisive comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: 'Just desert' and the gifts to be removed are not specified enough to settle whether the claim includes unending torment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges inability to work out the issue yet asserts certain justice on the basis of trust, producing a radical warrant-force mismatch.

charity.alternative: God may be righteous, but trust in that attribute does not demonstrate that the specified severe judgment is proportionate.
charity.decisiveQualification: The severity and duration of the outcome require an independent desert argument.

logicalCoherence.rationale: General trust in divine righteousness is compatible with justice but does not inferentially establish the proportionality of the challenged punishment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The speaker expressly substitutes faith for an unresolved reason and supplies no discriminating support for the punishment's severity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central design bridge by asserting deserved judgment and divine justice, despite leaving the comparison unresolved.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move appeals to general righteousness while omitting the strongest proportionality qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the loss a just desert, asserts that God will do right, and says that when reason cannot resolve the matter the speaker trusts God.

moves.speaker: Ray Comfort
moves.proposition: Belief in the resurrection is warranted by experiential revelation from the living Christ, which is promised to those who repent, obey, and trust Christ as their sin-bearer.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses the resurrection question to Ray, and the response's personal testimony and evangelical imperatives form one continuous answer.

components.text: Whether the resurrection and gospel foundations have a demonstrable, discriminating truth method rather than unsupported faith.
Whether promised experiential revelation accounts for sincere former believers or seekers who remain unconvinced.
Whether trusting Christ as sin-bearer supplies moral transformation rather than only liability payment.

response.rationale: Personal experience and a conditional scriptural promise are relevant purported evidence, but the move does not establish their reliability, independence, or ability to discriminate the resurrection from alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it offers issue-bearing experiential material but leaves the decisive reliability and demonstration demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: 'Manifested' and 'reveal' lack operational criteria, and the promise's scope over all repentant and trusting people is insufficiently bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A private experience and scriptural promise are treated as certainty of a public resurrection without addressing error, rival experiences, or failed cases.

charity.alternative: A sincere religious experience may be psychologically real without verifying the resurrection that the believer interprets it to reveal.
charity.decisiveQualification: Independent reliability and discrimination between competing interpretations are required.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The experience could support personal belief, but the bridge from subjective manifestation to historical resurrection and universal promise is substantially incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The evidence is private testimony plus scripture, without independent verification, adverse-case handling, or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central evidence burden by offering experiential revelation as warrant for the resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats the favored interpretation of experience as self-authenticating and omits the decisive alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says the risen Christ manifested himself to the speaker, quotes a promise of revelation, and conditions it on obedience, repentance, and trust.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The promised path to belief is insulated from failure when every sincere seeker who remains unconvinced can be blamed for seeking incorrectly or hardening their heart.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt begins immediately after Ray's resurrection answer and explicitly names Ray while analyzing the logical structure of Ray's promise to seekers.

components.text: Whether repentance and trust reliably produce experiential revelation confirming the risen Christ.
Whether nonbelief after apparent compliance can always be attributed to false conversion or improper seeking.
Whether the promised salvation path permits adverse experience to count against it.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the promise as insulated from failure because unsuccessful cases can be reclassified as hardened, insincere, or procedurally defective.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it identifies the decisive testability defect and states how adverse cases are excluded.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move specifies the conditional promise, the adverse case, and the available post hoc classifications that block disconfirmation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is tied to the observed structure of the preceding claims rather than asserted as a universal fact about every conversion account.

charity.alternative: Repentance and trust may have independent behavioral or dispositional criteria, allowing failed cases to be classified non-arbitrarily.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those criteria must be specified in advance and permit some sincere compliant failures to count against the promise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move clearly explains how defining every failure as improper compliance prevents the promise from facing adverse evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The earlier false-conversion diagnosis and immediate experiential promise specifically support the critique, though broader conversion practice is not surveyed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary falsifiability bridge at the top of the permitted tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly allows that independent criteria could avoid self-sealing while noting their absence here.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes a sincere seeker remaining unconvinced and explains how the model can answer by alleging a hardened heart or incorrect procedure.
